E1 – Circuit Tools and Semiconductor Physics (T0–T1, Week 1)

Why this matters in the exam: The circuit tools in this pack are what every later EDC question runs on. In the practice test, Q7(a) [4 marks] asks for the Thevenin equivalent “seen from the base of the transistor”. WS5 Q14 and Q15 open with the same step, and the diode and BJT questions (Q3, Q6–Q8, about 30 of the 50 marks) are KVL/KCL once the device is swapped for its model. Practice-test Q1 [5 marks] is concept MCQs, and Q1(I) is straight pn-junction physics. The test’s formula table lists , , , , and . WS2 Q2–Q7 are calculation questions that use exactly those formulas. So expect at least one short semiconductor calculation.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Circuit tools (WS1)

Tool What it is When to use it Common trap
KCL at a node Every node equation, nodal analysis Not drawing current arrows first (WS1 Remark 3.5.1)
KVL around a loop Base–emitter and collector loops later Sign errors. Go round in one direction and take each element’s polarity as you meet it
Voltage divider Only for elements in series (same current) Using it when a load hangs off the middle node. Then they are no longer in series
Current divider . For two resistors: Elements in parallel Putting the wrong resistor on top. The current through uses the other resistor
Superposition Sum of the responses to each independent source alone Linear circuits with several sources Turning off dependent sources (never do this). V source off means a short, I source off means an open
Thevenin = open-circuit voltage. = resistance seen with independent sources off Simplifying a bias network, e.g. a BJT base divider Forgetting to remove the load before finding
Norton = short-circuit current, , Source transformation (WS1 Q23) Getting the direction of wrong (arrow head = “+” of )
Nodal analysis KCLs written in node voltages Any circuit with 2+ unknown nodes A voltage source between two non-reference nodes needs a supernode
Mesh analysis KVLs in mesh currents Circuits with few meshes A current source on a boundary fixes that mesh current, so no KVL is needed there

Thevenin in three cases (WS1 §5.1):

  1. Only independent sources: switch them off and combine resistors.
  2. Independent and dependent sources: .
  3. Only dependent sources: apply a test source, then .

The bias-node Thevenin (you need this for BJT voltage-divider bias). Suppose a node X is connected to supply through , to supply through , and so on. Then

A resistor to ground counts as a “supply” of 0 V. This is just nodal analysis (KCL at X) with X open-circuited. For the standard divider ( to , to ground) it reduces to

Passive vs active sign convention (WS1 Q4, Q8, Q9, Q12). Passive: current enters the + terminal, means the element absorbs power. Active (sources): current leaves the + terminal, means the element supplies power. A resistor always has .

DC steady state: a capacitor acts as an open circuit and an inductor as a short circuit (WS1 Q6, Q7).

1.3 Semiconductor physics (Week 1 Part 2 slides, WS2)

Quantity Formula Use it when Trap
Intrinsic concentration , with , eV, eV/K Any temperature other than 300 K Using in J/K with in eV. Use eV/K here. T must be in kelvin
Room-temp value at 300 K Default when T = 300 K The formula gives . Use the given 1.5e10

Drift current density
Diffusion , Qualitative: carriers flow from high to low concentration The electron diffusion current flows opposite to the electron flow
Einstein relation Converting to
Thermal voltage , with J/K and Every diode or BJT exponential 27 °C gives 25.875 mV ≈ 26 mV. Some workshop solutions round to 25 mV

Mobility values. The lecture slide (Week 1 Part 2, slide 20) uses and , which gives and kΩ-cm. WS2 uses and , which gives and kΩ-cm. Always use the values the question gives you.

Doping. Group V atoms (P, As, Sb) are donors and make n-type material. Group III atoms (B, Al, Ga, In) are acceptors and make p-type material. Doped material is still electrically neutral (WS2 Q1 VII): each free carrier is balanced by a fixed ionised dopant. Majority carriers come from doping. Minority carriers come from thermal generation, so they are very temperature sensitive.

1.4 The pn junction, qualitatively

  • Open circuit. Majority carriers diffuse across the junction and recombine. This leaves fixed ionised dopants: + ions on the n side and − ions on the p side. That is the depletion region. Its field sets up the barrier , which opposes further diffusion and drives the minority-carrier drift current . At equilibrium , so there is no net current.
  • Charge balance. , so . The depletion region extends further into the lightly doped side. Typical is 0.1–1 µm.
  • Built-in voltage (standard Sedra form, consistent with slide 34): . For example, , gives V.
  • Forward bias (p side +): the barrier is lowered, shrinks, and the current rises exponentially.
  • Reverse bias: the barrier is raised and grows. Only flows (nA). does not depend on the voltage but doubles for every 10 °C rise.
  • Breakdown: beyond the PIV/PRV, avalanche or Zener mechanisms take over.

2. The method

2.1 Recognising the question type

You see… It is… Go to
“Thevenin equivalent seen from the base / node X” Bias-node Thevenin 2.2
A circuit with 2+ unknown node voltages, or “using nodal analysis” Nodal 2.3
“Using superposition” or two supplies feeding a node Superposition (or Millman) 2.2 / 2.4
or given, “find n, p” Carrier concentration 2.5
A bar or cylinder with dimensions, “find R / drift velocity” Resistance of a semiconductor 2.6
A temperature in °C with not given formula first 2.5
A concept MCQ (depletion, drift, diffusion, majority) Use the physics in 1.4 2.7

2.2 Thevenin at a bias node

  1. Redraw with the device (base, load) removed, leaving node X open.
  2. List every branch from X: (supply voltage, resistor). Ground is 0 V.
  3. : replace every supply by a short, so every branch goes to ground. all branch resistors in parallel.
  4. : KCL at X with nothing connected: , so . Or use superposition, one supply at a time.
  5. Draw the equivalent: in series with , then reconnect the device.
  6. Sanity check: must lie between the most negative and most positive supply.

2.3 Nodal analysis

  1. Choose the reference node (the one with the most branches, usually ground).
  2. Label the unknown node voltages.
  3. Any node joined to the reference by a voltage source is known, so it needs no KCL.
  4. A voltage source between two unknown nodes forms a supernode. Write one KCL around both nodes, plus .
  5. Write the KCL at each remaining node with currents leaving: .
  6. Put the equations in matrix form and solve (with a calculator matrix mode or by elimination).
  7. Back-substitute to find the currents you need. Check that KCL balances at one node.

2.4 Superposition

  1. Keep one independent source and switch the others off (V source → short, I source → open). Leave dependent sources in.
  2. Solve the simpler circuit with dividers.
  3. Repeat for each source and add the results with signs, using one consistent reference direction.

2.5 Carrier concentrations

  1. Find : use 1.5e10 at 300 K, otherwise compute with T in K.
  2. Identify the type: donors give n-type, acceptors give p-type.
  3. Compare with the doping. If doping ≥ 10 , use majority ≈ doping and minority = .
  4. If not, use the exact quadratic (table 1.3).
  5. Check that and that majority > minority.

2.6 Resistance of a semiconductor bar

  1. Convert all lengths to cm.
  2. Find n and p (method 2.5).
  3. , then .
  4. A = cross-section perpendicular to the current. L = length along the current.
  5. . If a voltage is given: , , .

2.7 Concept MCQs

  1. Underline the condition: unbiased, forward or reverse bias, n- or p-type, temperature up or down.
  2. Ask “which carriers, which mechanism?” Diffusion comes from majority carriers and a concentration gradient. Drift comes from minority carriers and the field.
  3. Eliminate the absolutes (“all”, “everywhere”, “permanently”). These are usually wrong in this course’s MCQs.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Leaving lengths in mm or µm. ρ is in Ω-cm, so convert: 1 mm = 0.1 cm, 1 µm = cm, and an area of 3 µm × 3 µm = cm² (not ).
  • Using in with in eV. Use eV/K there. Use the J/K value only in .
  • Forgetting the kelvin conversion. 50 °C is 323 K. Putting 50 into gives nonsense.
  • Forgetting the minority term or the check. Writing “” for doped material is wrong. In doped material , not .
  • Using the approximation when (light doping or high T). The minority carrier can then come out larger than the majority. If it does, use the exact formula.
  • Thevenin with the load still connected, or finding with a supply still “on”. Every supply on a bias node goes to ground when you find , including a negative rail.
  • Using the voltage divider on a loaded node. is only the open-circuit voltage. Once base current flows you must include (N3 shows a 10 % error).
  • Sign slips in KVL/KCL. Pick a direction and stick to it. A negative answer just means the true direction is opposite (WS1 Q3, Q20).

5. Practice

From your course files

Do these in order (about 45 min): WS1 Q1–Q12 concepts (6 min), Q13–Q19 (8 min), Q20–Q23 (8 min), Q24–Q25 (7 min), WS2 Q1 (3 min), WS2 Q2–Q4 (6 min), WS2 Q5–Q7 (7 min), then practice test Q1 (3 min). Official solutions exist for WS1 and WS2. The practice test has none, so it is worked here.

Workshop 1: circuit principles

WS1 Q1 (course question). When there are more electrons than protons in a piece of wire, we say it has a ———— charge.
a) Negative
b) Positive
c) Neutral
d) Not enough information to answer

Solution

a) Negative. More electrons than protons means a net negative charge.

WS1 Q2 (course question). In Figure 1, is positive if positive charges are moving to the ———— or negative charges are moving to the ————.
a) Left, Right
b) Right, Right
c) Left, Left
d) Right, Left

Solution

d) Right, Left. Conventional current is the flow of positive charge, so (arrow pointing right) is positive when positive charges move right, or equivalently when negative charges move left.

WS1 Q3 (course question). If our assumption about the higher potential end is wrong, the potential difference (voltage) will turn out to be ————.
a) Positive
b) Zero
c) Negative
d) Not enough information to answer.

Solution

c) Negative. A wrongly guessed polarity just gives a negative answer. The magnitude is still right.

WS1 Q4 (course question). Note the Passive sign convention for Ohm’s law, Current flows from the higher potential to the lower potential end. Therefore, charge carriers ———— potential energy by moving from the ———— end of the voltage to the ———— end. The energy is ———— by the resistor.
a) Lose, Positive, Negative, Absorbed
b) Lose, Negative, Positive, Absorbed
c) Absorb, Positive, Negative, Released
d) Absorb, Negative, Positive, Released

Solution

a) Lose, Positive, Negative, Absorbed. A resistor always absorbs energy and dissipates it as heat, so carriers lose potential energy going from + to −.

WS1 Q5 (course question). In a resistor with current , the power is ————.
a) Always negative
b) Always positive
c) Negative or positive
d) Negative or positive or zero

Solution

b) Always positive (official answer). If then too, so . Strictly , and it is zero when .

WS1 Q6 (course question). In a capacitor, if the voltage is constant, current is zero, and the capacitor is ———— to DC.
a) Short circuit
b) Open circuit
c) Constant voltage source
d) Either open or short circuit depending on the voltage magnitude

Solution

b) Open circuit. when is constant, and zero current is an open circuit.

WS1 Q7 (course question). In an inductor, if the current is constant, voltage is zero, and the inductor is ———— to DC.
a) Short circuit
b) Open circuit
c) Constant current source
d) Either open or short circuit depending on the voltage magnitude

Solution

a) Short circuit. when is constant, and zero voltage is a short circuit.

WS1 Q8 (course question). In the voltage source shown in Figure 5, current is assumed to flow from ———— potential end to the ———— potential end. If the source is supplying energy, will be ————.
a) Low, High, Positive
b) High, Low, Negative
c) Low, High, Negative
d) High, Low, Positive

Solution

a) Low, High, Positive. Active sign convention: current flows from the − end to the + end inside the source, and a source that supplies energy has positive .

WS1 Q9 (course question). In the current source shown in Figure 6, if the source is supplying energy, will be ————. Positive current leaves ———— end of the voltage.
a) Positive, Negative
b) Positive, Positive
c) Negative, Positive
d) Negative, Negative

Solution

b) Positive, Positive. In the active convention a supplying source has , and positive current leaves the + end.

WS1 Q10 (course question). Identify the type of dependent/controlled sources from left to right in Figure 7.

Solution

From left to right: VCVS (), CCVS (), VCCS (), CCCS (). Diamond with ± means a voltage source. Diamond with an arrow means a current source. The controlling variable is or .

WS1 Q11 (course question). What does short circuit mean? Select all correct options.
a) Zero potential difference
b) zero current
c) 0 Ω resistance
d) 0 S conductance
e) infinite resistance
f) infinite conductance

Solution

a, c, f. A short has zero voltage, zero resistance and infinite conductance. Its current is whatever the circuit sets.

WS1 Q12 (course question). Which statement(s) is(are) correct about Passive Elements? Select all correct options.
a) Deliver power when
b) Deliver power when
c) Absorb power when
d) Absorb power when

Solution

a, c. A charged capacitor or inductor can give energy back. With the passive convention it delivers when and absorbs when .

Workshop 2: semiconductor basics

WS2 Q1 (course question). Answer the following true or false questions by discussing them in your group: (please note that IX and X are related to diode):
I. At absolute zero temperature, the semiconductor behaves as a conductor.
II. No free electron or hole exists at absolute zero temperature.
III. At room temperature with thermal agitation, we have enough electrons and holes in a silicon wafer to have conductance.
IV. Holes are the majority charge carriers in a p-type semiconductor.
V. A hole is defined as the absence of an electron.
VI. A pure silicon has four valence electrons.
VII. A doped semiconductor is electrically charged at room temperature.
VIII. Diffusion current is the electric current caused by the charge carriers when they move from a higher concentration region to a lower concentration region.
IX. In an unbiased PN junction, the drift/saturation and diffusion currents are equal.
X. In the boundary of the two adjacent layers in a PN junction, we have the depletion layer and barrier voltage.

Solution

I F (it is an insulator at 0 K). II T. III F (intrinsic Si is not a conductor). IV T. V T. VI T. VII F (doped material is neutral: every free carrier is balanced by a fixed ionised dopant). VIII T. IX T. X T.

Practice test

PT Q1 (practice test, 5 marks). Circle the correct answer in the following multiple-choice questions (I to V).
I. When a PN junction is formed, why does a depletion region develop near the junction?
a) Electrons and holes recombine near the junction, leaving behind ionized dopants
b) The semiconductor becomes electrically insulating everywhere
c) All free electrons move from the N-region into the P-region permanently
d) The applied voltage removes all charge carriers from the semiconductor
II. The small-signal or dynamic resistance of a diode is related to:
a) The slope of the I–V characteristic at the operating point
b) The total length of the diode leads
c) The reverse breakdown voltage only
d) The DC supply resistance only
III. The main advantage of full-wave rectification over half-wave rectification is that full-wave rectification:
a) Uses only the negative half of the input waveform
b) Uses both half-cycles of the input waveform
c) Completely eliminates ripple without a capacitor
d) Requires no semiconductor devices
IV. Why is the base region of a BJT made relatively thin?
a) To allow most injected carriers to cross the base and reach the collector
b) To prevent carriers from reaching the collector
c) To increase the base resistance as much as possible
d) To eliminate the depletion region at the collector-base junction
V. Why are DC and AC analyses of a transistor amplifier often performed separately?
a) A transistor can operate with either DC or AC but never both
b) DC analysis establishes the operating point, while AC analysis examines small variations around that point
c) AC analysis determines the transistor’s doping concentration
d) DC analysis is only needed when the transistor is damaged

Solution

(I) Answer: a. Electrons and holes recombine near the junction and leave behind ionised dopants. (b) is wrong because the bulk still conducts. (c) is wrong because only carriers near the junction cross, and equilibrium stops further flow. (d) is wrong because a depletion region exists with no applied voltage at all.

(II) Answer: a. is the inverse slope of the I–V curve at the Q-point. This is covered in pack E2.

(III) Answer: b. Full-wave rectification uses both half-cycles.

(IV) Answer: a. A thin, lightly doped base means few injected electrons recombine, so most reach the collector (WS4 §3.2).

(V) Answer: b. The DC analysis fixes the Q-point. The AC analysis studies the small variations about it.

Solution N1

I – b. . Option (d) is itself, and (a) is , which applies only to intrinsic material.

II – b. At equilibrium, the majority-carrier diffusion current is balanced by the minority-carrier drift current . Carriers do cross the junction, so (a) is wrong. The depletion region holds only bound ions, so (d) is wrong.

III – c. Charge balance gives , so . The region extends into the lightly doped n side.

IV – b. Short . Both resistors then run from the base to ground, in parallel.

V – a. These are the two ideal-op-amp rules (WS4 §2).

E1 - CIRCUIT TOOLS + SEMICONDUCTOR PHYSICS
Divider (series only): Vi = Vin*Ri/Rsum   Current div (2 R): I1 = I*R2/(R1+R2)
Thevenin: Voc with load removed; RTh = R seen with V->short, I->open
  dep. sources present: RTh = Voc/Isc ; only dep.: RTh = Vtest/Itest
  IN = VTh/RTh, RN = RTh
Bias node X fed by (Vk,Rk), ground = 0 V branch:
  VTh = sum(Vk/Rk)/sum(1/Rk)    RTh = R1||R2||...
  Divider: VTh = VCC*R2/(R1+R2), RTh = R1||R2  -> then base KVL:
  VTh = IB*RTh + VBE + IE*RE
Nodal: ref node, KCL (leaving = source in), V-src between nodes -> supernode
Superposition: one indep. source at a time; dep. sources stay ON
Ideal op-amp: v+ = v-, i+ = i- = 0, no KCL at output; Vo limited by rails
-------------------------------------------------------------
ni = B T^1.5 exp(-Eg/2kT)  B=7.3e15, Eg=1.12 eV, k=8.62e-5 eV/K, T in K
ni(300K) = 1.5e10 cm^-3 ; ni^2 = 2.25e20
n0*p0 = ni^2 (equilibrium)
n-type: n ~ ND, p = ni^2/ND ; p-type: p ~ NA, n = ni^2/NA
Exact (n-type): n = ND/2 + sqrt((ND/2)^2 + ni^2), p = ni^2/n  (if ni >~ 0.1 ND)
sigma = q(n mu_n + p mu_p) (ohm-cm)^-1 ; rho = 1/sigma ; R = rho L/A (cm!)
vd = mu E, E = V/L ; J = sigma E ; D/mu = VT (Einstein)
mu: WS uses 1350/500, lecture slide 1300/500 -> use what is given
VT = kT/q, k = 1.38e-23 J/K, q = 1.6e-19 ; 27C -> 25.875 mV
1 um = 1e-4 cm ; 1 um^2 = 1e-8 cm^2 ; 1 mm = 0.1 cm
pn junction: open ckt ID (diffusion, majority) = IS (drift, minority)
  xn/xp = NA/ND (extends into lightly doped side), W ~ 0.1-1 um
  V0 = VT ln(NA ND / ni^2) ; FB: W shrinks, I exp ; RB: W grows, only IS
  IS doubles per 10 C ; doped material is electrically NEUTRAL
